name: Chaos Monkey

status.note: No code changes since October 2024 (last release v2.1.3, January 2025), though Netflix’s lifecycle file still marks it active.

summary: Netflix’s original chaos tool: on weekdays it picks instances at random from each app managed by Spinnaker and terminates them, so teams build services that survive losing a machine.
intro: Chaos Monkey does one thing: it terminates virtual machine instances and containers in production at random. It isn’t a service but a Go binary run by cron. Once each weekday a schedule job decides which instances will die that day and writes the terminations into a cron file; a terminate job then kills each one at its time, starting at a configured hour in a configured time zone so that engineers are at work when it happens.

Version 2 is built on Spinnaker, Netflix’s continuous delivery platform, and only works for apps deployed with it. Spinnaker supplies the list of instances, and each app turns Chaos Monkey on in Spinnaker’s config tab. There the owner sets the mean time between terminations (default two days) and the minimum time between them (default one day), and whether a group is the whole app, a stack or a cluster. Accounts, regions or stacks can be excluded. Chaos Monkey keeps its schedule and termination history in MySQL. It can also be told to stand down during outages, but only through an outage checker you write yourself in Go against its `Outage` interface.
strengths: Simple and blunt: random instance loss on a schedule is the most common failure in a cloud, and it forces every service to cope with it
Runs only in working hours on weekdays, with per-app frequency and opt-outs, so teams can start gently
Works on any cloud Spinnaker deploys to, and has been tested with AWS, Google Compute Engine and Kubernetes
limits: Requires Spinnaker and a MySQL database; without Spinnaker it can’t find or terminate anything
Only kills instances: no latency, network, resource or dependency faults, which Netflix split off from version 2.0
Little maintenance: the last code change was in October 2024, with open issues asking whether the project is retired
No steady-state check of its own: it terminates on schedule whether or not the service is healthy, unless you write and compile in an outage checker

story: When Netflix moved its streaming service to AWS, it designed every system to keep working when the systems it depended on failed. In a December 2010 post on lessons from the move, John Ciancutti wrote that “the best way to avoid failure is to fail constantly”, and that one of the first systems Netflix engineers built on AWS was the Chaos Monkey, whose job was “to randomly kill instances and services within our architecture”.

In July 2011 Netflix described a Simian Army that grew from it: Latency Monkey, Conformity Monkey, Doctor Monkey, Janitor Monkey, Security Monkey, 10-18 Monkey and Chaos Gorilla, which simulated losing a whole Availability Zone. Chaos Monkey was open-sourced on July 30, 2012, as part of the Simian Army; it found AWS Auto Scaling Groups and killed one instance per group, by default on non-holiday weekdays between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m., and in the previous year it had terminated over 65,000 instances.

In October 2016 Netflix released Chaos Monkey 2.0, now written in Go, run as a cron job and driven through Spinnaker, so it could reach AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and Cloud Foundry. It dropped the SSH-based faults, such as burning CPU or disabling a disk, which Netflix considered too “insidious” to inject at random. The older Simian Army repository was later archived. The project has had few changes since; its last commits, in October 2024, updated it for MySQL 8.0.

choices.why: Netflix wanted to find out that an app couldn’t survive losing an instance when people were around to fix it, not when paged at 3 a.m., and wanted to keep checking as code changed week to week.
Most apps were built to survive an instance going away, but for those that weren’t, Netflix wanted engineers alert and able to respond, so the schedule ran only on weekdays during the working day.
If an app owner did nothing, Chaos Monkey acted on the app, which made resilience the default. The open-source version also offered opt-in, for organisations testing the water.
Using Spinnaker’s view of deployments let one tool reach every cloud Spinnaker supports, instead of Chaos Monkey talking to AWS Auto Scaling Groups directly.
